solution:
Here the A.P. part is \(2, 4, 6, 8, \ldots\) (\(a = 2\), \(d = 2\)) and the G.P. part is \(1, x, x^2, \ldots\) (\(r = x\)), so \(t_n = 2n\,x^{n-1}\).
Let \(S_n = 2 + 4x + 6x^2 + \ldots + 2n\,x^{n-1}\).
Then \(x S_n = 2x + 4x^2 + \ldots + 2(n-1)x^{n-1} + 2n\,x^n\).
Subtracting, \((1-x)S_n = 2 + 2x + 2x^2 + \ldots + 2x^{n-1} - 2n\,x^n\), and the bracket is a G.P. of \(n\) terms with first term \(2\) and ratio \(x\):
\((1-x)S_n = \dfrac{2\left(1 - x^{n}\right)}{1-x} - 2n\,x^{n}\)
\(\therefore S_n = \dfrac{2\left(1 - x^{n}\right)}{(1-x)^{2}} - \dfrac{2n\,x^{n}}{1-x}\)
Equivalently, \(S_n = \dfrac{2\left(1 - n x^{n}\right)}{1-x} + \dfrac{2x\left(1 - x^{n-1}\right)}{(1-x)^{2}}\), which is the form printed in the book (check: at \(n = 2\) both give \(2 + 4x\)).
\(S_n = \dfrac{2\left(1 - n x^{n}\right)}{1-x} + \dfrac{2x\left(1 - x^{n-1}\right)}{(1-x)^{2}}\)

The A.P. part is \(1, 4, 7, 10, \ldots\) (\(a = 1\), \(d = 3\)) and the G.P. part has ratio \(r = x\), so \(t_n = (3n-2)x^{n-1}\).
Let \(S_n = 1 + 4x + 7x^2 + \ldots + (3n-2)x^{n-1}\).
Then \(x S_n = x + 4x^2 + \ldots + (3n-5)x^{n-1} + (3n-2)x^{n}\).
Subtracting, \((1-x)S_n = 1 + 3x + 3x^2 + \ldots + 3x^{n-1} - (3n-2)x^{n}\), where \(3x + 3x^2 + \ldots + 3x^{n-1}\) is a G.P. of \(n-1\) terms:
\((1-x)S_n = 1 + \dfrac{3x\left(1 - x^{n-1}\right)}{1-x} - (3n-2)x^{n}\)
\(\therefore S_n = \dfrac{1 - (3n-2)x^{n}}{1-x} + \dfrac{3x\left(1 - x^{n-1}\right)}{(1-x)^{2}}\)
(Check at \(n = 2\): this gives \(\dfrac{1 + 3x - 4x^{2}}{1-x} = 1 + 4x\).)
\(S_n = \dfrac{1 - (3n-2)x^{n}}{1-x} + \dfrac{3x\left(1 - x^{n-1}\right)}{(1-x)^{2}}\)

The terms are \(1, 2 \times 3, 3 \times 3^{2}, 4 \times 3^{3}, 5 \times 3^{4}, \ldots\), so \(t_n = n \cdot 3^{\,n-1}\) (A.P. part \(1, 2, 3, \ldots\); G.P. ratio \(r = 3\)).
Let \(S_n = 1 + 2 \cdot 3 + 3 \cdot 3^{2} + \ldots + n \cdot 3^{\,n-1}\).
Then \(3S_n = 3 + 2 \cdot 3^{2} + \ldots + (n-1) \cdot 3^{\,n-1} + n \cdot 3^{n}\).
Subtracting, \(S_n - 3S_n = 1 + 3 + 3^{2} + \ldots + 3^{\,n-1} - n \cdot 3^{n}\)
\(-2S_n = \dfrac{3^{n} - 1}{2} - n \cdot 3^{n}\)
\(\therefore S_n = \dfrac{n\left(3^{n}\right) - 1}{2} + \dfrac{3 - 3^{n}}{4} = \dfrac{(2n-1)3^{n} + 1}{4}\)
(Check at \(n = 3\): \(\dfrac{5 \cdot 27 + 1}{4} = 34 = 1 + 6 + 27\).)
\(S_n = \dfrac{n\left(3^{n}\right) - 1}{2} + \dfrac{3 - 3^{n}}{4}\)

Write each term as (A.P. term) \(\times\) (G.P. term): \(3 = 3 \cdot 2^{0}\), \(12 = 6 \cdot 2\), \(36 = 9 \cdot 2^{2}\), \(96 = 12 \cdot 2^{3}\), \(240 = 15 \cdot 2^{4}\). So \(t_n = 3n \cdot 2^{\,n-1}\) (A.P. part \(3, 6, 9, \ldots\); ratio \(r = 2\)).
Let \(S_n = 3 + 12 + 36 + \ldots + 3n \cdot 2^{\,n-1}\).
Then \(2S_n = 6 + 24 + \ldots + 3(n-1) \cdot 2^{\,n-1} + 3n \cdot 2^{n}\).
Subtracting, \(S_n - 2S_n = 3 + 6 + 12 + \ldots + 3 \cdot 2^{\,n-1} - 3n \cdot 2^{n}\)
\(-S_n = 3\left(2^{n} - 1\right) - 3n \cdot 2^{n}\)
\(\therefore S_n = 3n \cdot 2^{n} - 3 \cdot 2^{n} + 3 = 3\left[(n-1)2^{n} + 1\right]\)
(Check at \(n = 4\): \(3\left[3 \cdot 16 + 1\right] = 147 = 3 + 12 + 36 + 96\).)
\(S_n = 3\left[(n-1)2^{n} + 1\right]\)

The terms are \(1, \dfrac{2}{4}, \dfrac{3}{16}, \dfrac{4}{64}, \ldots\), i.e. \(t_n = n\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{n-1}\), so \(a = 1\), \(d = 1\), \(r = \dfrac{1}{4}\). Since \(|r| < 1\) the sum to infinity exists.
For an arithmetico-geometric series, \(S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r} + \dfrac{dr}{(1-r)^{2}}\).
\(S_\infty = \dfrac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{4}} + \dfrac{1 \cdot \frac{1}{4}}{\left(1 - \frac{1}{4}\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{9}{16}} = \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{4}{9}\)
\(S_\infty = \dfrac{16}{9}\)

Expand the general term: \((r+1)(2r-1) = 2r^{2} + r - 1\).
\(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r+1)(2r-1) = 2\sum r^{2} + \sum r - \sum 1 = 2 \cdot \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} + \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} - n\)
\(= \dfrac{n}{6}\left[2(n+1)(2n+1) + 3(n+1) - 6\right] = \dfrac{n}{6}\left[4n^{2} + 6n + 2 + 3n + 3 - 6\right]\)
(Check at \(n = 3\): \(\dfrac{3(36 + 27 - 1)}{6} = 31 = 2 + 9 + 20\).)
\(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r+1)(2r-1) = \dfrac{n\left(4n^{2} + 9n - 1\right)}{6}\)

Split the sum term by term:
\(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(3r^{2} - 2r + 1\right) = 3\sum r^{2} - 2\sum r + \sum 1 = 3 \cdot \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} - 2 \cdot \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} + n\)
\(= \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{2} - n(n+1) + n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left[(n+1)(2n+1) - 2(n+1) + 2\right]\)
\(= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2n^{2} + 3n + 1 - 2n - 2 + 2\right]\)
Check by direct addition: \(n = 1\) gives \(2\) and the formula gives \(\dfrac{1}{2}(2+1+1) = 2\); \(n = 2\) gives \(2 + 9 = 11\) and the formula gives \(\dfrac{2}{2}(8+2+1) = 11\); \(n = 3\) gives \(33\) and the formula gives \(\dfrac{3}{2}(18+3+1) = 33\).
[Textbook answer-key error: the book prints \(\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2n^{2} + 2n + 1\right)\), which is incorrect — at \(n = 1\) it gives \(\dfrac{5}{2}\), not even a whole number, and at \(n = 2\) it gives \(13\) instead of \(11\).]
\(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(3r^{2} - 2r + 1\right) = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(2n^{2} + n + 1\right)\)
_note: PRINTED KEY IS WRONG. Book gives n/2 (2n^2 + 2n + 1); correct is n/2 (2n^2 + n + 1). Verified by direct summation: n=1 true 2 vs book 5/2; n=2 true 11 vs book 13; n=3 true 33 vs book 75/2; n=4 true 74 vs book 82; n=5 true 140 vs book 305/2. Book form 0/5, corrected form 5/5.

solution:
The numerator of the general term is the sum of the first \(r\) natural numbers, so \(1 + 2 + 3 + \ldots + r = \dfrac{r(r+1)}{2}\).
Hence the \(r\)th term is \(\dfrac{1}{r} \cdot \dfrac{r(r+1)}{2} = \dfrac{r+1}{2}\).
\(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac{r+1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\sum r + \sum 1\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} + n\right] = \dfrac{n}{4}\left[(n+1) + 2\right]\)
(Check at \(n = 3\): \(\dfrac{3 \cdot 6}{4} = \dfrac{9}{2} = 1 + \dfrac{3}{2} + 2\).)
\(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{1+2+\ldots+r}{r}\right) = \dfrac{n(n+3)}{4}\)

The numerator of the general term is \(1^{3} + 2^{3} + \ldots + r^{3} = \left[\dfrac{r(r+1)}{2}\right]^{2} = \dfrac{r^{2}(r+1)^{2}}{4}\).
So the \(r\)th term is \(\dfrac{r^{2}(r+1)^{2}}{4\,r(r+1)} = \dfrac{r(r+1)}{4} = \dfrac{r^{2} + r}{4}\).
\(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\dfrac{r^{2}+r}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} + \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right] = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{24}\left[(2n+1) + 3\right] = \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+4)}{24}\)
(Check at \(n = 3\): \(\dfrac{3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5}{12} = 5 = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{3}{2} + 3\).)
\(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{1^{3}+2^{3}+\ldots+r^{3}}{r(r+1)}\right) = \dfrac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{12}\)

Use \(a^{2} - b^{2} = (a+b)(a-b)\). In every bracket the two numbers are consecutive, so \(a - b = 1\) and the bracket equals \(a + b\).
Hence \((70^{2} - 69^{2}) + (68^{2} - 67^{2}) + \ldots + (2^{2} - 1^{2}) = (70 + 69) + (68 + 67) + \ldots + (2 + 1)\)
\(= 70 + 69 + 68 + \ldots + 2 + 1 = \dfrac{70 \times 71}{2}\)
The sum is \(2485\).

The \(r\)th term is \(t_r = (2r-1)(2r+1)(2r+3) = \left(4r^{2} - 1\right)(2r+3) = 8r^{3} + 12r^{2} - 2r - 3\).
\(S_n = 8\left[\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^{2} + 12 \cdot \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} - 2 \cdot \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} - 3n\)
\(= 2n^{2}(n+1)^{2} + 2n(n+1)(2n+1) - n(n+1) - 3n\)
\(= n\left[2n(n+1)^{2} + 2(n+1)(2n+1) - (n+1) - 3\right] = n\left[2n^{3} + 4n^{2} + 2n + 4n^{2} + 6n + 2 - n - 4\right]\)
\(= n\left(2n^{3} + 8n^{2} + 7n - 2\right) = n(n+2)\left(2n^{2} + 4n - 1\right)\)
Check by direct addition: \(n = 1\) gives \(15\) and the formula gives \(1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 = 15\); \(n = 2\) gives \(15 + 105 = 120\) and the formula gives \(2 \cdot 4 \cdot 15 = 120\); \(n = 3\) gives \(120 + 315 = 435\) and the formula gives \(3 \cdot 5 \cdot 29 = 435\).
[Textbook answer-key error: the book prints \(n^{2}(n+1)^{2} + \dfrac{8n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} + \dfrac{3n(n+1)}{2}\), which is the sum of \(r(2r+1)(2r+3)\), i.e. it uses first factor \(r\) in place of the printed \(2r-1\). It agrees at \(n = 1\) (both \(15\)) but gives \(85\) at \(n = 2\) and \(274\) at \(n = 3\), against the true \(120\) and \(435\).]
\(S_n = n(n+2)\left(2n^{2} + 4n - 1\right)\)
_note: PRINTED KEY IS WRONG. Book prints n^2(n+1)^2 + 8n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 + 3n(n+1)/2, which is the closed form of the sum of r(2r+1)(2r+3) — the book used first factor r where the question prints 2r-1. Verified by direct summation: n=1 true 15 vs book 15 (AGREES — a spot-check at n=1 would certify the wrong answer); n=2 true 120 vs book 85; n=3 true 435 vs book 274; n=4 true 1128 vs book 670; n=5 true 2415 vs book 1385. Book form 1/5, corrected form 5/5.

solution:
Numerator: \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} r(r+1) = \sum r^{2} + \sum r = \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} + \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} = \dfrac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3}\).
Denominator: \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n} r = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\).
So the ratio is \(\dfrac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{n(n+1)} = \dfrac{2(n+2)}{3}\).
Given \(\dfrac{2(n+2)}{3} = \dfrac{100}{3}\), so \(2(n+2) = 100\), i.e. \(n + 2 = 50\).
\(n = 48\)
